title: Conditional Types
summary: **Conditional types** let a type choose between two outcomes with `T extends U ? X : Y` — and with `infer` you can pattern-match and extract pieces of a type, which is how `ReturnType`, `Parameters`, and `Awaited` are built.

subtopics.title: The conditional form: T extends U ? X : Y
subtopics.explanation: A conditional type is a type-level ternary. It asks 'is T assignable to U?' — if yes the type resolves to X, otherwise to Y. This lets a type's result depend on another type, e.g. type IsString<T> = T extends string ? true : false produces the literal true or false depending on what you pass.
subtopics.example: type IsString<T> = T extends string ? true : false;

subtopics.title: The infer keyword
subtopics.explanation: Inside the extends clause, infer X introduces a fresh type variable that TypeScript solves for by pattern-matching the structure. type ElementType<T> = T extends (infer U)[] ? U : never extracts the element type of an array. infer is how you pull a piece out of a larger type instead of just testing it.
subtopics.example: type ElementType<T> = T extends (infer U)[] ? U : never;

subtopics.title: Distributive conditional types
subtopics.explanation: When the checked type is a naked type parameter and you pass a union, the conditional distributes over each member: T extends U ? X : Y applied to A | B becomes (A extends U ? X : Y) | (B extends U ? X : Y). This is why Exclude<'a' | 'b', 'a'> yields 'b' — it filters the union member by member.
subtopics.example: type NonNull<T> = T extends null | undefined ? never : T;

subtopics.title: Turning off distribution with [T]
subtopics.explanation: Sometimes you want to treat the whole union as one unit instead of distributing. Wrapping both sides in a one-element tuple, [T] extends [U] ? X : Y, defeats distribution because the checked type is no longer a naked parameter. This is the standard trick for whole-union checks like IsNever.

subtopics.title: Building ReturnType from scratch
subtopics.explanation: ReturnType combines extends with infer: type ReturnType<T> = T extends (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : never. It matches any function type, captures the return type as R via infer, and yields it. Parameters and InstanceType are built the same way, inferring different positions.
subtopics.example: type ReturnType<T> = T extends (...a: any[]) => infer R ? R : never;

subtopics.title: Nested and composed conditionals
subtopics.explanation: Conditionals can be chained like else-if ladders: T extends A ? X : T extends B ? Y : Z. They also compose with mapped types and recursion to express rich transformations, such as a deep Readonly or unwrapping nested promises. Keep them readable — deep nesting hurts both humans and the compiler.
subtopics.example: type TypeName<T> = T extends string ? 'string' : T extends number ? 'number' : 'other';

foundations.overview: A conditional type selects between two result types based on an assignability test, and with the infer keyword it can also extract sub-types from the type being tested. Together they make TypeScript's type system able to compute new types from existing ones — testing, filtering unions, and unwrapping structures — entirely at compile time.
foundations.formalDefinition: A conditional type has the form T extends U ? X : Y, resolving to X if T is assignable to U and to Y otherwise. Within the U position, infer V binds a fresh type variable to a matched portion of the structure. When T is a naked type parameter and a union is supplied, the conditional distributes across each union member.
foundations.whyItMatters: Conditional types power the higher-order utility types (ReturnType, Parameters, Exclude, Extract, NonNullable, Awaited) and let libraries express precise return types that depend on their inputs. In interviews they test whether you can program at the type level, not just annotate values.
foundations.mentalModel: Read T extends U ? X : Y as a type-level if/else: 'if T fits the shape U, use X, else use Y.' Read infer R as 'capture whatever type appears in this slot and call it R.' Distribution is the type-level map over a union.
foundations.browserPerspective: Conditional types are purely compile-time. They are evaluated by the type-checker and erased before emit, producing no JavaScript and adding nothing to bundle size or runtime behavior in the browser.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Deriving a hook's return type from its arguments, unwrapping Promise<T> to T (Awaited), filtering union members (Exclude/Extract), flattening nested arrays, and writing overload-aware return types for generic helpers like a typed event emitter.
foundations.businessImpact: Precise, input-dependent types catch integration mistakes at compile time, so misused APIs fail in the editor rather than in production, reducing incident and debugging cost.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Library authors can express one generic function whose return type adapts to its input, sparing consumers from manual casts and giving the whole team accurate autocomplete across a large surface area.
foundations.performanceImpact: No runtime cost. Deeply nested, recursive, or widely-distributed conditional types can significantly slow the type-checker and editor, so bound recursion and prefer the simplest conditional that expresses the rule.
commonUseCases: Extracting a function's return or parameter types (ReturnType/Parameters)
Pattern-matching structure with infer to flatten or unwrap types

commonMisconceptions.myth: T extends U ? X : Y always evaluates U against T as a whole.
commonMisconceptions.reality: When T is a naked type parameter and a union is passed, the conditional distributes over each member; wrap in [T] extends [U] to check the union as a single unit.

commonMisconceptions.myth: infer can be used anywhere in a type to grab a value.
commonMisconceptions.reality: infer is only valid inside the extends clause of a conditional type, where it pattern-matches a position in the checked structure.

config.intro: Trace type ReturnType<T> = T extends (...a: any[]) => infer R ? R : never with greet: (n: string) => number.

steps.name: Substitute T
steps.detail: T becomes the function type (n: string) => number, the type of greet.

steps.name: Match the shape
steps.detail: TypeScript checks T against the pattern (...args: any[]) => infer R — a function with some return.

steps.name: Infer R
steps.detail: The infer R slot binds to the function's return type, so R = number for this call.

steps.name: Pick the branch
steps.detail: Because T matched a function, the conditional resolves to the true branch, which is R.

steps.name: Resolve the type
steps.detail: ReturnType<typeof greet> evaluates to number — the captured return type.

codeLab.title: Implement ElementType<T> with infer
codeLab.instructions: Write a conditional type ElementType<T> that, when given an array type, resolves to its element type using infer, and otherwise resolves to never. ElementType<number[]> should be number.
hints: Test whether T is an array of some element type with T extends (infer U)[].
Return the captured U in the true branch and never otherwise.

debuggingLab.title: Unexpected distribution over a union
debuggingLab.symptom: A conditional meant to test 'is T exactly never?' returns the wrong answer (or never) because the naked parameter distributes over the union instead of being checked as a whole.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Because T is a naked type parameter, the conditional distributes over unions — and never is treated as the empty union, so distributing over it yields never instead of true. The test is evaluating member-by-member rather than against the whole type.
commonMistakes: Forgetting that a naked type parameter distributes over unions.
Not accounting for never behaving as the empty union under distribution.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Disable distribution so the union (and never) is checked as a single unit, making IsNever<never> resolve to true.

theory.question: What is a conditional type and how does it work?
theory.directAnswer: A conditional type is a type-level ternary of the form T extends U ? X : Y: it resolves to X when T is assignable to U and to Y otherwise. This lets a type's result depend on another type — the basis for utilities like Exclude, NonNullable, and ReturnType — and it is fully evaluated by the compiler and erased at emit.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A type whose result is chosen by an assignability test between two types.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To compute one type from another — filtering, branching, and extracting — instead of writing every variant by hand.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The checker tests T against U; if assignable it yields X, otherwise Y. With a naked type parameter and a union input, the conditional distributes across members; infer in the U slot captures matched sub-types.

theory.whyImportant: Conditional types are the engine behind higher-order utility types and a core advanced-TS interview topic that reveals type-level programming ability.
theory.realWorldExample: NonNullable<T> = T extends null | undefined ? never : T strips null and undefined from a type, e.g. for a value already past a null check.

nestedTopics.title: Assignability test
nestedTopics.explanation: extends asks whether T is assignable to U, not whether they are equal.

nestedTopics.title: Distribution
nestedTopics.explanation: A naked type parameter distributes the conditional over each union member.

nestedTopics.title: infer
nestedTopics.explanation: Captures a sub-type from the checked structure inside the extends clause.

followUps.question: Does extends mean equality here?
followUps.answer: No — it tests assignability (is T a subtype of U), so 'a' extends string is true even though they are not the same type.

followUps.question: Do conditional types cost anything at runtime?
followUps.answer: No — they are evaluated at compile time and erased, emitting no JavaScript.

theory.question: What does the infer keyword do, and where can it be used?
theory.directAnswer: infer declares a fresh type variable inside a conditional type's extends clause and lets TypeScript solve for it by pattern-matching the structure being checked. For example T extends (infer U)[] ? U : never captures an array's element type. It can only appear in the U position of a conditional and is how ReturnType, Parameters, and Awaited extract pieces of a type.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A placeholder bound by the compiler to whatever type occupies a matched position in the checked structure.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To extract sub-types (return types, element types, promise payloads) rather than merely test for them.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: During the assignability check, the compiler unifies the pattern containing infer against T, binding each infer variable to the matched type; the true branch can then reference those variables.

theory.whyImportant: infer is the difference between testing a type and decomposing one; understanding it signals deep type-system fluency in interviews.
theory.realWorldExample: Awaited<T> uses recursive infer to unwrap Promise<Promise<string>> down to string.

nestedTopics.title: Position matters
nestedTopics.explanation: infer is only valid inside the extends clause of a conditional type.

nestedTopics.title: Multiple infers
nestedTopics.explanation: You can infer several variables at once, e.g. both parameters and return of a function.

followUps.question: Can you infer more than one type at a time?
followUps.answer: Yes — e.g. T extends (a: infer A) => infer R ? [A, R] : never captures both the parameter and the return type.

scenario.question: A util type Flatten<T> is supposed to return T[] elements when T is an array and T otherwise, but for union inputs it behaves unexpectedly. What is happening and how do you control it?
scenario.directAnswer: The conditional is distributing over the union because the checked type is a naked parameter, so Flatten is evaluated separately for each member and the results are unioned — which may not be what you want for a whole-union decision. If you want per-member behavior, distribution is correct; if you want to treat the union as a single unit, wrap both sides in tuples ([T] extends [U]) to disable distribution.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Diagnosing and controlling distributive behavior of a conditional type over union inputs.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Distribution is the default for naked type parameters and is often desirable (Exclude/Extract), but it surprises people doing whole-union checks.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Naked T distributes; wrapping in a one-element tuple makes the checked type non-naked, so the union is tested as one unit.

scenario.whyImportant: Distribution is the single most common source of confusing conditional-type results; controlling it deliberately is a key skill.

nestedTopics.title: When to keep distribution
nestedTopics.explanation: Filtering union members (Exclude, Extract, NonNullable) relies on it.

nestedTopics.title: When to disable it
nestedTopics.explanation: Whole-union checks like IsNever or matching a union as one shape need the [T] trick.

followUps.question: How exactly do you disable distribution?
followUps.answer: Wrap both the checked type and the compared type in single-element tuples: [T] extends [U] ? X : Y.

coding.question: Implement Awaited-style UnwrapPromise<T> that recursively unwraps nested Promise types to the final resolved type, and demonstrate it.
coding.thoughtProcess: I need a conditional that matches Promise<infer U> and, if U is itself a promise, keeps unwrapping. So the true branch should recurse: if T is Promise<infer U> then UnwrapPromise<U>, else T. This handles Promise<Promise<string>> by peeling one layer per recursion until a non-promise remains.
coding.lineByLine: UnwrapPromise<T> tests T extends Promise<infer U>: infer U captures the resolved type. The true branch recurses with UnwrapPromise<U> so nested promises peel layer by layer; the false branch returns T unchanged. A resolves Promise<Promise<string>> to string; the runtime await mirrors this by resolving both promises.
coding.timeComplexity: Type-level recursion proportional to nesting depth; runtime is a single await chain.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(depth) of type-instantiation; negligible at runtime.

alternativeApproaches.title: Use the built-in Awaited
alternativeApproaches.explanation: TypeScript ships Awaited<T>, which also handles thenables, so prefer it in real code.

followUps.question: Why does the true branch reference UnwrapPromise again?
followUps.answer: Because a promise can resolve to another promise; recursing unwraps every layer until the inner type is no longer a Promise.

systemDesign.question: Design the type layer for a type-safe event emitter where on(event, handler) and emit(event, payload) must enforce that each event's payload type matches a central registry. How do conditional types and inference make this safe?
systemDesign.directAnswer: Define a single EventMap interface mapping each event name to its payload type as the source of truth. Type on<K extends keyof EventMap>(event: K, handler: (payload: EventMap[K]) => void) and emit<K extends keyof EventMap>(event: K, payload: EventMap[K]), using indexed access EventMap[K] so the payload type is derived from the event key. Conditional types layer in extra rules — for example a conditional that allows omitting the payload argument when EventMap[K] is void/undefined — and infer can extract a handler's payload type from existing listener signatures. The compiler then rejects any mismatched event/payload pair at the call site.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A typed pub/sub API whose method signatures derive payload types from a central event registry, refined by conditional types.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: String-keyed emitters are stringly-typed and error-prone; deriving payloads from one map makes every emit/on call checked.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Generic key parameters constrained to keyof EventMap plus indexed access EventMap[K] tie payloads to events; conditional types handle special cases (no-payload events), and infer can pull payload types out of handler signatures.

systemDesign.whyImportant: Event systems are a classic place where loose typing causes runtime bugs; designing a registry-driven, conditional-type-aware API is a strong advanced-TS interview demonstration.

nestedTopics.title: Registry as source of truth
nestedTopics.explanation: One EventMap drives every method's payload type via indexed access.

nestedTopics.title: Conditional optional payloads
nestedTopics.explanation: A conditional can make the payload argument optional when EventMap[K] is void.

nestedTopics.title: infer from handlers
nestedTopics.explanation: infer can extract a listener's payload type to relate on/emit signatures.

followUps.question: How do you let emit omit the payload for events with no data?
followUps.answer: Use a conditional on the payload parameter — e.g. ...args: EventMap[K] extends void ? [] : [payload: EventMap[K]] — so no-data events accept no payload argument.

followUps.question: How does this stay maintainable as events grow?
followUps.answer: Adding an entry to EventMap automatically types on and emit for that event; no method signatures need editing, keeping the API in lockstep with the registry.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Conditional types sit in the type-utility layer of a codebase, enabling generic functions whose return types adapt to inputs and centralized type transforms (unwrapping, filtering, decomposing). Library boundaries especially benefit, exposing precise types to consumers without forcing casts.
productionDeepDive.performance: Zero runtime cost. The danger is compile-time: recursive conditionals (deep unwrapping), wide distribution over large unions, and heavy nesting can slow tsc and the editor markedly. Bound recursion depth, avoid distributing over huge unions, and alias complex results.
productionDeepDive.security: Conditional types describe shapes and cannot validate runtime data. A precise type derived from an external response is still only a compile-time claim, so untrusted input must be validated at runtime regardless of how exact the conditional type is.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Express each transform once (UnwrapPromise, ReturnType-like helpers, union filters) and compose them; this keeps the type layer DRY as the API surface grows, with input-dependent types updating automatically.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Prefer built-in conditional utilities (ReturnType, Parameters, Exclude, Extract, NonNullable, Awaited) before writing your own. Keep custom conditionals shallow, name them by intent, and comment distribution behavior, since the [T] trick and infer placement are easy to misread.
productionDeepDive.observability: Type errors surface in the editor and in CI via tsc --noEmit. For tricky conditionals, hover to inspect the resolved type and add type-level test assertions (Expect/Equal) so refactors that break a conditional fail fast.

caseStudies.problem: Developers needed return/parameter extraction, promise unwrapping, and union filtering generically.
caseStudies.solution: Shipped ReturnType, Parameters, InstanceType, Awaited, Exclude, Extract, and NonNullable — all conditional types using extends and infer.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Extremely expressive, but recursive/distributive conditionals can degrade compiler and editor performance.
caseStudies.lessons: Most input-dependent typing needs can be met by composing the built-in conditional utilities rather than authoring bespoke ones.

projectBuilder.summary: Use conditional types and infer to build a type-safe action layer for the Expense Tracker: derive handler return types and filter the action union.
requirements: A central ExpenseAction discriminated union as the source of truth
A ReturnType-style helper to derive a reducer's output type
An Exclude-based filter to separate write actions from read actions
An UnwrapPromise helper for the async API layer
projectBuilder.architecture: A types module exports conditional-type utilities: ActionOf<T> filters the action union, ReducerResult<T> uses ReturnType to type the reducer output, and Resolved<T> unwraps promises from the API client so callers get the awaited type.

src/

  lib/

steps.title: Action union
steps.instructions: Define ExpenseAction = AddAction | RemoveAction | LoadAction with a 'type' discriminant.
steps.checkpoint: All actions share a literal discriminant field.

steps.title: Filter actions
steps.instructions: Use Exclude to derive WriteAction (everything except LoadAction).
steps.checkpoint: WriteAction excludes the read action via distribution.

steps.title: Reducer result type
steps.instructions: Derive the reducer's state type with ReturnType<typeof reducer>.
steps.checkpoint: The store type stays in sync with the reducer automatically.

steps.title: Unwrap API promises
steps.instructions: Write Resolved<T> = T extends Promise<infer U> ? U : T for the API client.
steps.checkpoint: await results are typed without manual annotations.

enhancements: Add a conditional that makes payload-less actions omit their payload field
Add a deep Awaited-style unwrap for nested promise responses
interviewQuestions: Why does Exclude correctly drop a single action variant from the union?
How would infer let you extract each action's payload type into a lookup type?

keyTakeaways: A conditional type is a type-level ternary: T extends U ? X : Y, resolving by assignability.
infer (inside the extends clause) captures sub-types — the basis of ReturnType, Parameters, and Awaited.
Naked type parameters distribute the conditional over each union member; wrap in [T] extends [U] to disable it.
Conditionals compose with mapped types and recursion to filter, unwrap, and decompose types.
They are erased at runtime — prefer the built-in conditional utilities and keep custom ones shallow for compiler speed.
